analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices directly and offer its own government-run prescription drug plan.
analysis.headline: The bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices and run its own drug plan was referred to two House committees in January 2009, sent to a health subcommittee the next day, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a Medicare-operated prescription drug plan starting in 2010, offered nationwide alongside the private drug plans that currently serve Medicare enrollees. The government plan would negotiate purchase prices directly with drug manufacturers and use a scientifically reviewed formulary to steer toward lower-cost, clinically effective drugs. It would also guarantee an appeals process for beneficiaries denied a non-formulary drug, and it directed the government to tell every beneficiary that the public option existed.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries. Anyone enrolled in Part D could choose a government-run plan whose drug costs were set through direct negotiation with manufacturers rather than by private insurers. The bill required a single national premium based on the plan's average cost, and it used independent clinical review (through the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality) to pick drugs on the basis of both benefit and price. Beneficiaries denied a drug would get a defined appeals process, including external review, with medical necessity decided by professional judgment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors enrolled in Medicare drug coverage

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated drug plans covering the entire United States beginning in 2010, as an alternative to private plans [S3].

Directs the Secretary to negotiate with pharmaceutical manufacturers over the purchase price of covered drugs and to use strategies similar to other federal purchasers, such as the VA, to lower costs [S3].

Requires the plan's drug formulary to be built on clinical effectiveness assessments, favoring drugs that cost less and work as well or better, with tiered copays, generic substitution, and other value tools [S3].
Creates an appeals process for denials, including initial review by the Secretary and external review by an independent entity, so beneficiaries can get medically necessary non-formulary drugs [S3].
Requires the government to inform all beneficiaries of the public plan's existence through the annual Medicare handbook and the Medicare website [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue would fall as the government negotiated prices and steered patients toward lower-cost and generic equivalents. Private Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers would face a government competitor for enrollment in the program they currently run exclusively.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug manufacturers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The formulary tools the bill authorizes — tiered copays, prior authorization, step therapy, reference pricing — could delay or restrict access to some drugs for enrollees in the public plan, even though the bill includes medical-necessity appeals and an exemption process [S3].

Negotiated prices and competitive bidding on formulary placement would reduce revenue for brand-name drug makers, a cost an honest supporter would weigh against possible effects on investment in new medicines [S3].

The formulary cannot change mid-year except in narrow cases (new generics, safety removals, major new treatments), which could leave enrollees waiting for access to a newly useful drug until the next plan year [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors, the benefit is direct: a drug plan whose prices are negotiated by the government and whose coverage decisions are grounded in independent clinical review, with a guaranteed appeals process. The costs fall mainly on the pharmaceutical industry in the form of lower prices, and the main risk to patients is that cost-control tools like prior authorization and step therapy could slow access to some drugs — a risk the bill tried to manage with medical-necessity appeals and an external review option. The bill's design leans toward patient protection, though its price-negotiation power depended entirely on how aggressively a future administration used it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, sent to the Energy and Commerce health subcommittee the next day, and sat there until the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Marion Berry (D-AR) introduced the bill on January 26, 2009, joined by 13 original cosponsors including Reps. Schakowsky, Frank, Kennedy, Van Hollen, and McCollum [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, for portions within its jurisdiction, to the Ways and Means Committee [S5].
On January 27, 2009, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health [S5].
That was the last recorded action; the bill never advanced out of subcommittee and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

The bill text shows the core mechanism: a Medicare-run drug plan, nationwide, with the Secretary negotiating directly with manufacturers and using a clinically reviewed formulary to cut purchase costs [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and the private insurers that administer Medicare Part D. Because the bill died without a vote, the government kept the existing arrangement in which Medicare is barred from directly negotiating drug prices and private plans remain the only channel for the benefit — so beneficiaries continued paying drug prices set without government negotiation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Rep. Marion Berry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a Medicare-operated drug plan with direct price negotiation with manufacturers [S1, S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee of first referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or floor consideration; the bill was referred to the Health Subcommittee on January 27, 2009 and no further action was recorded before the Congress ended [S5].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the second committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup appears in the action history [S5].

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices, defending the Medicare Part D structure that bars direct government negotiation — the arrangement this bill would have changed.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats, 28 of the 253 House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a vote where the full chambers' party split could be measured [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required the government to negotiate purchase prices directly and to use a value-based formulary steering patients toward cheaper, clinically equivalent drugs — cutting manufacturer revenue on Medicare drugs. The industry's interest ran against beneficiaries' interest in lower drug prices.

industries.industry: Private Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Private plans currently hold exclusive control of the Medicare drug benefit under a law barring Medicare from negotiating prices; a government-run competing plan with negotiated prices would draw enrollment away and could pressure their pricing. The bill's failure preserved their exclusive role.
